## 2026-10-09T15:27:56.638Z — Assistant

Segment: 01a12012-6bd4-7681-9f97-1b59a739ff3b

Yes—we can preserve the look closely while making the walls react.

We’d export **6K surface maps** from Blender—colour, roughness and normals—then recreate its satin material in R3F. Real-time lights would produce moving highlights, and local reflection captures would reflect changing surroundings. Three.js supports [physical materials](https://threejs.org/docs/pages/MeshPhysicalMaterial.html) and [real-time reflection captures](https://threejs.org/docs/pages/CubeCamera.html).

We’d carefully match the blue spill, warmth and contrast against Blender. **The same vibe is achievable; 100% identical Cycles rendering at every angle isn’t guaranteed.** Simply adding reflections over the current bake would double-count lighting, so we’d replace that approach.

## 2026-10-11T18:49:40.079Z — Assistant

Segment: 01a12012-6bd4-7681-9f97-1b59a739ff3b

**We have a strong cinematic foundation, but it isn’t submission-ready yet.**

What works well:
- The dark opening and gradual lighting return create atmosphere.
- The screen → theatre → projector sequence gives the camera movement a purpose.
- The materials and amber lighting feel consistent.

From an Awwwards perspective, visual impact alone isn’t enough—they evaluate **design, usability, creativity and content**. [Evaluation overview](https://www.webdesignawards.io/awards/awwwards)

My honest priorities now:

- **Content and typography:** the blank screens need a compelling story.
- **Navigation:** visitors should immediately understand scrolling and where it leads.
- **Performance:** smooth behavior on ordinary laptops and phones still needs verification.
- **Projector presentation:** its dark face loses detail; we should eventually make the focal object easier to read.

The direction is promising. The next big improvement should be **turning this beautiful scene into a clear, complete experience**, rather than adding more effects.

## 2026-10-14T08:48:40.297Z — User

Segment: 01a12012-6bd4-7681-9f97-1b59a739ff3b

1. Massive File Size (355 MB): Your site is trying to download the equivalent of a short movie before it even starts. Your desktop computer has fast internet and a strong graphics card to handle this, but your laptop runs out of memory (VRAM) and crashes.
2. Overloaded Graphics Card: Your site forces the computer to process 7.3 million triangles and calculate reflections simultaneously. This completely suffocates normal laptop hardware.
3. The "Wait for Everything" Gate: Your code is designed to block the user until every single high-quality texture and shader is fully ready.
Awwwards judges will give a failing score to a site that takes minutes to load or crashes a laptop.

How to Fix It (Straight to the Point)


1. Fix the Crashes (Reduce Graphics Strain)

• Cap the Resolution: Force the site to run at a maximum Device Pixel Ratio (DPR) of 1.5 instead of 2. This instantly cuts out millions of unnecessary pixel calculations.
• Turn off 4x MSAA: Disable hardware multi-sampling. Use a lightweight post-processing anti-aliasing shader (like FXAA) instead.
• Simplify the Models: Your projector model has 1.5 million triangles. Crush that asset down to under 50,000 triangles using a 3D optimization tool.

2. Fix the Load Time (Stop Making Users Wait)

• Shrink the Reflection Files: The "Theatre floor reflections" file is 59 MB alone. Resize all reflection textures down to a fraction of their current size (e.g., 512x512) and blur them slightly so they still look good.
• Don't Load Everything Upfront: Change your loading screen logic. Load only the low-quality assets needed for the first 5 seconds of the intro. Let the high-quality textures stream in quietly in the background while the user is already looking at the site.
• Combine the Seating: Use GPU Instancing for the seats. This tells the computer to load the math for one single seat and copy it 20 times, rather than loading 5.7 million individual triangles all at once.

Also, We need to compress every glb model, texture and reduce triangle. 

Talk to me

- **Remove unnecessary passes and invisible work** before changing appearance.
- **Reduce the expensive assets/materials identified by those comparisons.**
- **Add adaptive quality:** lower rendering resolution and reflection detail on weaker devices while preserving composition, colours and animation.

The sofa reduction was useful, but **small model files do not guarantee cheap rendering**.

Our practical target should be **60 FPS where possible, stable 30 FPS on weaker supported devices**, with a fast first usable view. We can work toward an award-quality experience; an Awwwards win cannot be guaranteed.

## 2026-10-15T15:25:19.272Z — User

Segment: 01a12012-6bd4-7681-9f97-1b59a739ff3b

**What "many-angle reflection" means**

In real life, a surface changes as you walk around it. The wooden floor shines strongly when you look along it, and dimly from above. The wall fabric gets a soft sheen when you look at it from the side.

A normal baked texture is **one photo, taken straight on**. It looks the same from every angle, so the shine can't move when the camera moves.

So for some theatre surfaces, your Blender scripts did more: they **captured each surface from many directions, one image per direction**. The site blends those images while you move, so the shine changes exactly like in Blender.

**Where it is**

| Model | What it covers | Directions | File | Size |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Floor (`floor.glb`) | walnut floor, step fronts, side faces | 81 | `floor-views.ktx2` | 17.7 + 5.1 MB preview |
| Walls (`walls.glb`) | left, right, front wall | 49 | `walls-views.ktx2` | 9.9 + 2.9 MB preview |
| Seat tables (`seat-tables.glb`) | small tables between sofas | 25 | `seat-tables-views.ktx2` | 4.6 + 1.4 MB preview |
| **Total** | | | | **41.6 MB** |

Smaller versions of the same idea:
- **Ceiling:** 5 directions, about 3 MB.
- **Moon:** 69 directions through the glass plus 25 backing captures, about 4.5 MB.

**What's happening, step by step**

1. **In Blender, done earlier:** for each surface, Cycles rendered the light from every direction: straight on, then rings tilted at 30°, 45°, 60°, 70°, 80° and 86°, with 8 or 16 directions around each ring. Each result was saved as "how much brighter or darker than straight-on", one 512×512 image per direction.
2. **On the site, loading:** it downloads the main straight-on bake (4K) plus the direction images.
3. **On the site, every frame, for every pixel:**
   - It works out the angle the camera sees that point from.
   - It finds the 2 nearest rings and the 2 nearest directions, and reads those 4 images (up to 8).
   - It blends them and applies the result to the main bake.
   - On the floor, it also handles the walnut plank joints separately.

**Advantages**
- **Very close to Blender from any camera angle:** the floor shine and wall sheen move correctly.
- **Real-looking materials:** the walnut floor and velvet walls look rich and real.
- **Cheap to draw:** under 1 ms per frame on my desktop. It's not one of the 4 lag causes.

**Disadvantages**
- **Big download:** 41.6 MB, about 18% of the whole site.
- **Graphics memory:** about 80 MB, which matters on phones.
- **Slow to update:** any change to these surfaces in Blender means re-capturing every direction, which takes hours.
- **Complex code:** hard for anyone else to edit.

**Fix options**

| Option | What | Download | Look | Blender work |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | Low uses the 256-px versions already on the server | 41.6 → 9.4 MB | almost the same at screen size | none |
| **B** | Fewer directions, cut from the existing files (for example floor 81 → about 40) | about half | shine slightly less exact at low angles | none |
| **C** (rebuild) | One bake per surface plus a normal glossy material that reflects the room | about 2 MB | shine still moves, close to Blender but not exact | one simple bake |

**My recommendation:** option A now, because it's fast, safe, and Ultra stays identical. Option C if you rebuild.

Research finished. **Your idea is achievable as a convincing visual illusion on a normal screen.** The best approach combines cinema-style filtering with carefully prepared depth layers. I haven’t changed the site.

I saved the detailed findings and implementation plan here: [Cinema-glasses research](</D:/New folio/new site code/new_site_three/docs/cinema-glasses-research.md>).

**What the physics tells us**

Real cinema glasses separate two projected eye views. They remove the unwanted view rather than sharpen a blurry image. A phone recording through one lens can therefore capture a cleaner picture, but it doesn’t capture the audience’s binocular depth experience. [Barco’s explanation](https://www.barco.com/de/news/news-insights/2016-03-03-can-you-watch-3d-with-one-eye-closed)

Your reference’s third, faint blue outline is something we can reproduce artistically. It isn’t a requirement of stereoscopic projection. Also, ghost separation should depend on an object’s depth **relative to the screen plane**—not simply “farther objects get more blur.” [Barco’s ghosting analysis](https://www.barco.com/en/news/news-insights/2017-02-20-of-ghosts-and-screens)

From the supplied still, I can infer the likely visual mechanism. I cannot confirm its projector technology, whether editing contributed to the effect, or how it behaves in motion.

**What makes it feel dimensional**

The clear image alone won’t be enough. We need several cues working together:

- The character overlaps the landscape.
- Distant mountains have softer contrast and atmospheric haze.
- Foreground and background move slightly differently.
- The glasses have visible thickness, highlights and perspective.

These cues can convey depth even through one eye. That is why they remain useful on an ordinary website. [Depth-perception reference](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK11512/), [motion-parallax research](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4901450/)

My design recommendation is to make the clear-versus-ghosted difference immediately understandable, then use subtle movement to strengthen the depth. Strong blur everywhere would hide the artwork rather than improve the illusion.

**The important refinement to our plan**

Both appearances must share the **same artwork, crop, scale and movement**.

Outside the lenses, we add depth-dependent ghost copies. Inside, those copies disappear. If the character moves slightly against the mountains, that movement must remain consistent across the lens boundary—otherwise the glasses will look like windows into a different picture.

**What we actually need**

| Item | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Lightweight glasses model | Frame, bridge, temples and two lens surfaces |
| One composition in roughly 3–4 aligned layers | Background, mountains/environment and foreground subject |
| Background filled behind the subject | Prevent holes when layers move |
| Layer masks; optional depth map | Control separation and ghost offsets |
| Small reflection/highlight asset | Give the lenses a believable surface |

Preparing hidden background matters: simply displacing a flat image can produce stretched edges or holes. Layered-depth research addresses precisely this problem. [CVPR 2020 project and examples](https://shihmengli.github.io/3D-Photo-Inpainting/)

**How I’d build ours efficiently**

Use the existing theatre once. Draw the ghosted screen normally, then reveal the clean screen imagery through masks matching the two lenses. Official drei documentation supports masking without rendering another complete scene. [Mask documentation](https://drei.docs.pmnd.rs/portals/mask)

For the opening:

1. Dim room, illuminated screen, glasses near the viewer.
2. Clear imagery through the lenses; controlled ghosting outside.
3. During the existing pullback, glasses move away and expose the ghosted image.
4. Projection fades while room lighting rises.
5. Remove the opening effect’s resources afterward.

I’d start with approximately **1,000–3,000 triangles for the glasses**, modest artwork resolution, and inexpensive lens highlights. Those are starting budgets—not performance promises.

The next decision is **the screen composition and how the glasses frame it**. Good artwork separation will contribute more to this effect than an expensive glass shader.

## 2026-10-21T06:59:38.400Z — Assistant

Segment: 01a12012-6bd4-7681-9f97-1b59a739ff3b

Finished the deeper research. **My earlier answer explained the principle, but it did not establish the reference’s exact layer count or blur settings.** Those cannot be recovered reliably from that small screenshot. :codex-annotation{index="1"}

The detailed findings are saved here: [Layers, blur and cinema-glasses research](</D:/New folio/new site code/new_site_three/docs/cinema-glasses-optics-deep-dive.md>).

**1. Without glasses: how many layers, which blur, how much?**

Real stereo cinema normally presents **two perspective views**, one for each eye. Without glasses, both become visible together. What looks blurry can actually be **two reasonably sharp images slightly displaced horizontally**. Edmund Optics explicitly explains this uncovered “fuzzy” appearance. [Engineering explanation](https://www.edmundoptics.com.tw/knowledge-center/video/tutorials/how-do-3d-movies-work-polarization/)

That distinction matters:

- Small separation can look like softness.
- Larger separation exposes recognisable duplicate outlines.
- A Gaussian blur alone cannot reproduce those distinct contours.

Experiments have investigated this transition between apparent blur and doubling. There is no single separation that produces the same appearance for every picture and viewing condition. [Original CMU research](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/afs/cs/project/sensor-9/ftp/papers/SPIE2001-4297-06t.pdf)

Your mountain’s “main image + faded blue image + faint outline” is therefore a useful **three-contribution visual treatment**. It is not proof that the original uses three source layers.

We must also separate the effects that your screenshot combines:

| Appearance | Likely mechanism |
|---|---|
| Shifted mountain outlines | Overlapping views |
| Soft distant landscape | Authored defocus, haze or reduced detail |
| Blue fringe | Filtering, recording or deliberate styling |
| Moving trails | Exposure/timing or motion effects |

Physical defocus depends on aperture and focus distance. Its shape is not automatically Gaussian; Gaussian blur is a convenient rendering approximation. [NVIDIA’s optical explanation](https://developer.nvidia.com/gpugems/gpugems3/part-iv-image-effects/chapter-28-practical-post-process-depth-field)

**2. Through premium glasses: how does it become one proper view?**

The glasses **separate the views; they don’t blur them together**:

1. The left lens passes primarily the left-eye picture.
2. The right lens passes primarily the right-eye picture.
3. The brain matches corresponding features and interprets their differences as depth.

Different objects retain different disparities. They do not all become aligned onto one flat depth plane. [Human-vision research](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3490636/)

Cinema systems achieve separation through polarization, wavelength filtering or synchronised shutters. Dolby, for example, uses projector-matched wavelength-separation glasses for its 6P system. [Dolby documentation](https://professional.dolby.com/product/dolby-cinema-imaging-products/dolby-3d-bundles/)

**There is no standard “premium glasses blur amount.”** Better separation means less unwanted image leakage, called crosstalk. Measurements show that leakage varies with the display, brightness and viewing conditions. It is a different quantity from blur. [Measured crosstalk study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5935021/)

If the mountain remains soft through the glasses, that can be softness already in the movie. The glasses cannot restore detail lost through genuine defocus.

**3. What this means for our opening**

I recommend **four aligned artwork groups**: sky, distant mountains, nearer landscape and subject. That gives us control over depth, softness and overlap.

For your uncovered appearance, this is a concrete **starting recipe to test—not a measurement of the reference**:

| Contribution | Mix weight | Additional Gaussian softness* |
|---|---:|---:|
| Main picture | 75% | None |
| Displaced cool ghost | 20% | 0.6–1 px |
| Faint displaced contour | 5% | 1.2–2 px |

*Values are Gaussian standard deviations at an artwork width of 1,000 pixels. They must scale with the displayed artwork. These weights are mixing coefficients, not physical crosstalk measurements.*

Inside the virtual lenses:

- Remove the ghost contributions.
- Preserve the same crop, size and artwork position.
- Preserve intentional mountain softness.
- Start with **zero additional overall lens blur**.
- Suggest depth through overlap and subtle relative movement.

A normal screen still gives both physical eyes substantially the same website image. Our result will reproduce the **visual impression of the reference**, rather than actual cinema stereopsis.

The research supports proceeding with this approach. **The next requirement is a well-prepared layered composition—not a more expensive glass shader.** No implementation changes have been made.

> - It must be considerably less noticeable than the second contribution. It should not look like a third full-strength logo or another readable line of text.
>
> **COMPOSITING RULES**
>
> - The **75/20/5 values are normalised mixing weights**, not three full-strength pictures stacked on top of one another.
> - Mix each layer’s contributions using premultiplied colour and alpha, then composite that result over the background.
> - Preserve the original layer order: background → decorations → text → logo.
> - Blur colour and alpha consistently to avoid dark or white fringes.
> - Do not duplicate the opaque white background along with a foreground object.
> - Do not introduce rectangles behind individual elements.
> - Keep the dominant image anchored to the clean master. Only its weaker copies move.
>
> **DO NOT ADD**
>
> - A glasses frame, lens shape, clear window or split-screen comparison. Those will be added later in the website.
> - Vertical displacement, rotation, stretching, perspective or magnification.
> - Strong red/cyan anaglyph colouring.
> - Bloom, lens flare, drop shadows, motion streaks or film grain.
> - New lettering, replacement fonts, changed logo details or extra decorations.
> - Global blur or global colour adjustments.
>
> **CHECK BEFORE EXPORT**
>
> 1. The main lettering and logo retain their original position and size.
> 2. The text is recognisable, with subordinate ghost edges.
> 3. The logo has the strongest separation; text has less; decorations have the least.
> 4. The background remains unchanged.
> 5. Ghosts are displaced horizontally, not merely softened in place.
> 6. There are no white boxes, dark halos or missing logo details.
>
> **DELIVERABLE**
>
> Export **`screen-ghosted.png`** as an opaque **2048 × 1152 PNG**, using the same colour profile as the clean master.
>
> Preserve **`screen-clean.png`** unchanged. Save the editable document with the original layers and ghost contributions separately named.
>
> **If precise layer operations are unavailable, report that limitation instead of regenerating the artwork.**

4. Check it through the **actual scroll movement**. One screenshot angle still has camera movement during the journey; we’ll support that movement without baking arbitrary orbit views.
5. Compare with Blender before accepting it.

## 2026-10-23T06:53:18.792Z — Assistant

Segment: 01a12012-6bd4-7681-9f97-1b59a739ff3b

**Yes—your suggestion is a sensible approach.** Export the floor’s material properties, then let the browser render them under matched lighting.

We would use:

- **Base colour:** wood colour and grain, without baked shadows.
- **Normal map:** small bumps and plank grooves.
- **Roughness:** where reflections are sharp or soft.
- **Clearcoat settings:** the polished finish.
- **Lighting/reflection environment:** matched to the theatre.

These material channels are supported by the PBR workflow. [Blender export documentation](https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/dev/addons/scene_gltf2.html)

**The difficulty is matching the lighting.** An HDRI provides surrounding illumination and reflections, but it won’t automatically reproduce nearby theatre lights, contact shadows and their exact floor reflections. The same textures alone cannot guarantee the same rendered image. [Three.js material documentation](https://threejs.org/docs/pages/MeshStandardMaterial.html)

Compared with my previous proposal, **PBR is better for reflections responding naturally as the camera moves**. A camera-specific bake is better at preserving one particular rendered appearance. :codex-annotation{index="1"}

**My recommendation:** use PBR maps as the foundation, match the theatre’s reflection environment, and add a small baked lighting map only if needed. No dozens of angle captures.

We should aim for **a visually indistinguishable result along your camera journey**, but I cannot promise literal 100% equality between Blender and the browser before testing. **Nothing changed yet.**

Yes—**compressed 6K can retain finer detail than 4K**, especially when viewed close up.

| | Compressed 6K | 4K |
|---|---|---|
| Fine detail | Potentially sharper | Less detail |
| GPU memory, same format | About 2.25× higher | Lower |
| Download size | Depends on compression | Usually smaller |
| Normal viewing distance | May look identical | May look identical |

But **strong compression can damage 6K enough that a cleaner 4K looks better**.

For our scene, the reported 6K benefit is mainly the **corridor floor and ceiling**. The smooth, dark walls showed little improvement. We should compare actual compressed results before choosing.

|---|---|
| How soon does something appear? | Which files and preparation block the opening |
| How long until everything is ready? | Total downloads, decoding and scene preparation |
| How smooth is movement afterward? | Drawing cost, effects, resolution and device power |

From the Active Theory code we inspected, it uses several approaches:

- **Prioritizes the first scene.** It has separate preparation paths for the opening and other scenes.
- **Spreads preparation over time.** Some texture and geometry uploads are distributed instead of doing everything in one blocking burst.
- **Adjusts work for the device.** Particle counts, rendering resolution and expensive effects vary with GPU capability.
- **Combines techniques.** Baked lighting, compressed textures and custom shaders each handle different parts of the appearance. One sampled wall-and-ceiling bake was only **1K and 57 KB**; that does not mean every texture is that small. 2. **Sofas:** preserve the colour you like. Add subtle leather grain and roughness variation so highlights feel softer and less plastic.

6. **Coloured slides:** finish them with materials matching the adjoining corridor walls, floor and trim. Remove the diagnostic colours.

7. **Formation lighting:** connect everything to one timeline using the previous project as reference: theatre/projector-area lights dim, the formation flash happens, illumination continues around the forming projector, then lighting returns smoothly. Because much of our lighting is baked into textures, changing scene lights alone won’t produce this—we must control the baked appearance too.

For smoothness, **7 seconds and no hangs is progress, but loading and animation smoothness are separate problems.** I’ll measure frame times during mirrors, camera travel, formation and assembly, then address the expensive code.

My order would be: remove curtain and finish slides → projector materials, particles and lighting → moon glass and sofa roughness → complete texture audit → performance verification.

**Yes—this could be a stronger transition.** A liquid sphere becoming the page gives the change from the corridor to the website a clear visual connection.

I checked the current code: the rectangle enters, the next scroll brings it closer, and another scroll expands it to fill the screen. We can keep those same steps and replace their visual treatment.

My suggestion:

1. **Arrival:** a pearl-white liquid sphere floats into the corridor. It gently stretches and settles, catching a little warm light from the environment.
2. **Next scroll:** it approaches and flattens into a rounded rectangle. One soft ripple travels across its surface as the corners become defined.
3. **Final scroll:** the rectangle expands to cover the screen. Its highlights disappear into the page background, and the actual HTML page takes over without a visible jump.

**The important improvement is continuity:** it should feel like the same material changing shape throughout. I would keep the movement controlled—one deformation and one settling ripple. Excessive wobbling could weaken the cinematic atmosphere.

From the development side, I would use a small procedural mesh with its shape animated on the GPU. This can avoid another large model or texture download. We should prepare its shader before arrival and stop rendering once the HTML page takes over. Detailed glass refraction can add significant rendering cost, so I’d start with carefully shaded liquid highlights. [Three.js material documentation](https://archive.threejs.org/docs/api/en/materials/MeshPhysicalMaterial.html)

For **Awwwards**, this is a promising creative detail, provided scrolling remains responsive and mobile performance holds up; their mobile guidance explicitly considers usability and performance. [Awwwards guidelines](https://www.awwwards.com/mobile-excellence-guidelines.pdf)

For **UK agency applications**, my judgment is that the strongest impression would come from the complete execution: distinctive motion, consistent art direction, clean page handoff and a smooth mobile version. The sphere alone won’t establish that.

**I recommend pearl-white liquid with subtle warm highlights**, connecting the dark cinematic corridor to the bright page. Prototype this transition alone first, keeping the rest of the journey intact.

## 2026-10-26T05:36:10.654Z — Assistant

Segment: 01a12012-6bd4-7681-9f97-1b59a739ff3b

**Yes, an animated model can be efficient.** It depends on how we build the animation.

| Approach | Benefit | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| **Blender model with shape keys** | Precise control over the sphere → rectangle shapes | Adds model and deformation data |
| **Procedural animation in code** | Small download; easy to adapt to screen size and scrolling | More shader work to get convincing liquid movement |
| **Exported fluid simulation** | Complex splashes and flowing detail | More data and complexity than this transition needs |

Shape keys store a few different shapes of the same mesh. The website smoothly blends between them; Three.js supports this through morph targets. [Three.js documentation](https://threejs.org/docs/pages/Mesh.html)

**For our transition, I recommend procedural animation.** We need one controlled sphere, a gentle liquid ripple and a clean rectangle—not a complex fluid event. That makes it a good fit for a small mesh animated in code.

If we need a very specific sculpted silhouette that is difficult to achieve procedurally, **Blender shape keys would be my second choice**. We can still control playback through scrolling.

Either way, the glossy material matters: a lightweight model can still render slowly with expensive reflections or refraction.

For agencies and Awwwards, I’d prioritize **beautiful motion, immediate scroll response and a seamless page handoff**. The implementation method should serve those results.

## 2026-10-26T13:40:02.470Z — Assistant

Segment: 01a12012-6bd4-7681-9f97-1b59a739ff3b

**I see a strong direction here: a physical board made from responsive metallic grains, with your logo as its centre.** The references give us three different ingredients: behaviour, shape and material.

From your screenshots:

| Reference | What I would take from it |
|---|---|
| **1 — Active Theory** | A dense particle world with depth, movement and recognisable forms. The logo gives the activity a clear centre. |
| **2 — the board** | Its broad, thin surface, defined edges and sense of a physical object occupying space. |
| **3 — the circled material** | Dark charcoal, fine texture and soft silver highlights. It reads closer to **textured gunmetal or graphite** than ordinary cement, although the screenshot cannot establish the actual material. |

The third image interests me most: the surface seems solid, but also looks capable of moving. **That could become our central idea.**

Imagine arriving at the final section:

1. **The camera reveals a shallow graphite board against the black background.** Light catches its bevel and reveals a dense granular surface. Your logo is immediately readable.
2. **Moving the pointer disturbs the grains locally.** They part, rise and settle with weight, like fine metallic material responding to pressure. On touch, a gentle drag produces the same response.
3. **Selecting something gives the particles a purpose.** They rise from the board into a recognisable object connected to that project, then return to the surface when dismissed.
4. **The logo remains the anchor.** We could retain restrained red, blue and yellow accents within its existing shapes, surrounded by the quieter steel material.

This would combine your references through one consistent material and behaviour.

My main disagreement would be with filling the entire screen with equally active particles. It could look impressive, but it could also hide the logo, compete with text and become visually tiring. **I would make the board densely reactive, with fewer drifting grains around it.** We can still achieve that feeling of abundance while giving the eye somewhere to rest.

I would also avoid another lengthy assembly entrance. We already have the projector forming. For this ending, I’d favour a short material reveal, followed by interaction that visitors control. That would give this section its own identity.

For the finish, my preference is **fine-grained graphite metal**: subtle irregularity, soft silver reflections and a narrow light along the edges. Keep the broad surface calm enough that it does not resemble noisy concrete. The logo also needs considerably clearer lighting than it has in your current screenshot.

On winning: this could strengthen the site, but we cannot estimate award chances from an effect alone. Awwwards currently weights design **40%**, usability **30%**, creativity **20%** and content **10%**. My interpretation is that the interaction should make your work easier to discover as well as memorable. [Official evaluation criteria](https://www.awwwards.com/about-evaluation/)

For agency hiring, I think that is the stronger demonstration too: visitors see your visual judgement, interaction design and ability to present actual work. We should also set a performance budget before building this, given the unresolved projector wait.

**The first decision I’d discuss with you is its purpose: should this be a final logo spectacle, or an interactive board where people explore projects and reach About/Contact?** I lean toward the interactive board—it gives the particles something meaningful to do.

## 2026-10-26T15:50:04.702Z — Assistant

Segment: 01a12012-6bd4-7681-9f97-1b59a739ff3b

Yes, I understand the marked image: **broad particle clouds above and below the eye opening**, with the logo visible in the clear centre. The particles should have depth and flowing movement across those filled regions.

I checked the code, official documentation and a working particle example. **Nothing has been changed.**

1. **The shape needs rebuilding.**  
   Currently, particles are concentrated around two narrow curves. We should spread them through the marked regions, using dense clusters, quieter gaps and softer outer edges. Simply thickening the lines would still look like an outline.

2. **The material needs refinement.**  
   The particles already have a material, but it uses round shapes and a simplified highlight. That explains the bead-like appearance. I recommend small, irregular metallic grains: dark charcoal bodies, restrained silver highlights, varied roughness and lighting consistent with the logo. Most should remain subtle, with occasional brighter grains showing the movement.

3. **For this effect, I recommend keeping GPU animation in the website.**  
   Drawing many particles together and calculating their movement on the graphics chip is an established approach. The [official R3F guidance](https://r3f.docs.pmnd.rs/advanced/scaling-performance) supports this batching strategy.

   Blender can help us design the composition, grain shapes and material reference. Exporting a complete Blender particle animation does **not automatically make it faster**. For example, glTF’s GPU-instancing extension does not directly provide individual instance animation; that needs additional application logic. [Khronos documentation](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF/blob/main/extensions/2.0/Vendor/EXT_mesh_gpu_instancing/README.md)

4. **Loading and smoothness need separate checks.**  
   This eye currently downloads no separate particle model or texture—the browser generates its particle data. However, shader preparation still takes time, and overlapping particles still cost graphics performance. A fuller field needs careful limits on particle size, overlap and shading, especially on phones. [WebGL performance guidance](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebGL_API/WebGL_best_practices)

   The earlier 75 FPS checks ran on this PC. They do **not** prove performance on your actual laptop or phone. Your reported projector-loading delay also remains unresolved.

My proposed next pass is **filled composition first, metallic appearance second, then real-device performance checks**. Mobile should retain the complete eye composition, with simpler shading and fewer carefully distributed grains.

Here is how that helps our eye idea.

**1. Our eye needs a body, not just an outline**

Your current draft draws particles along the eye’s upper and lower edges. You want the broad areas you marked to contain particles too.

Active Theory uses **three-dimensional point clouds**: collections of points with positions and colours. Those points occupy shaped spaces, with depth, dense areas and gaps.

For ours, we can create:

- A broad upper cloud and lower cloud.
- A clear eye-shaped opening between them.
- Our logo in the middle as the pupil.
- Dense clusters mixed with softer, scattered edges.

That gives us the full composition you wanted. Simply adding more particles to the existing thin lines would mostly make thicker lines.

**2. The expensive-looking material does not need a huge texture**

Their shared particle shading texture is only **64 × 64 pixels, about 2 KB**.

The richness comes from combining that small texture with particle colours, sizes, highlights and depth. Some particles catch the light; others sit quietly in shadow.

For ours, I suggest charcoal and muted silver particles, with occasional brighter highlights. That would suit the black background and future steel logo. We should avoid making every particle equally white and shiny—that is one reason particles can look artificial.

**3. We can make the cloud flow without moving thousands of objects individually**

Their shaders calculate particle movement on the **GPU—the graphics processor**.

In simple English: we give the graphics processor the points and rules for their movement. It draws them together, rather than JavaScript moving a separate object for every grain.

For our eye, the rules could create:

- A continuous left-to-right flow.
- Small swirling movements inside that flow.
- Gentle changes in density, so it feels alive.
- A restrained response to the pointer.

The overall eye should remain readable while the particles inside it move. If the entire shape constantly twists, we lose your idea.

Your thinking about attaching the eye to the logo is sound. We can place the cloud in the same coordinate system as the logo, so the existing camera moves around both together.

We can preserve your camera animation. The particle shape must be designed to work with it.

**5. Mobile can keep the design with fewer particles**

Their code changes particle counts, rendering resolution and optional effects according to device capability.

We should use the same principle: preserve the complete eye shape on every device, while reducing density and expensive effects where necessary.

Their workstation version drew over a million points, but **that is evidence of their technique, not a sensible target for ours**. We need to measure our scene, which already contains the theatre, corridor and projector.

Short version: in this section the `.bin` isn’t a 3-D *model* at all — it’s a **compressed bag of points** (positions + colours) that seeds the GPU particle sim. A normal model format (`.glb`/`.gltf`) would be the wrong tool here, and they even have both code paths side by side so you can see the choice.

### Why `.bin` and not `.glb` here

**1. The forest is never drawn as geometry, so mesh data would be dead weight.**\
A `.glb` carries triangle indices, normals, UVs, materials — everything you need to *render a surface*. This section renders **points**, not a surface. Proof: the loader returns only two attributes —

`app.beautified.js:29881`

return { positions: new AntimatterAttribute(data.positions, 3),          colors:    new AntimatterAttribute(data.colors, 3) };

That’s it. Positions + colours. No indices, no normals, no UVs. Shipping a `.glb` would mean shipping (and parsing) a bunch of fields the particle system throws away.

**2. Draco compression makes it tiny.** The `.bin` wraps a Draco stream (that’s what the whole first part of this project’s reverse-engineering established: `[10-byte length][JSON manifest][Draco stream]`). Draco is *built* for exactly this — compressing dense position/colour clouds — which is how the forest cloud drops from tens of MB to a few MB. The decoder is only pulled in when the file is binary:

`app.beautified.js:29869`

let data, isBinary = path.includes(".bin"); if (path = Assets.getPath(path), init(), isBinary)   await GeomThread.loadDracoLib(),                 // load the Draco wasm decoder   data = await Thread.shared().loadDraco({ type:"decode", path: … });

**3. The same choice lets them ship LOD variants.** Because it’s their own container, they can keep forest-128/256/512/1024.bin and pick one by device — that’s the `powerOf2` suffix (`app.beautified.js:31263`, files at `:10382-10394`). A single `.glb` wouldn’t give you that per-tier swap for free.

**4. The engine confirms it’s a deliberate fork, not a limitation.** The generic mesh path right next to it *does* use `.glb`/`.gltf` — so they chose `.bin` on purpose for particles:

`app.beautified.js:31994`

if (String(geomPath).indexOf(".glb") > 0 || String(geomPath).indexOf(".gltf") > 0) {   gltfNodes = await loader.parse(geomPath, …);   // GLB/GLTF → real mesh nodes } else geom = await GeomThread.loadGeometry(geomPath);  // .bin → Draco → geometry/points

`.glb` when they want a mesh; `.bin` (Draco point cloud) when they want a point field to simulate.

### How the `.bin` actually becomes the forest

1. **Decode in a worker** — `Thread.shared().loadDraco({type:"decode"})` runs off the main thread, so the big decode never stutters the render loop (`app.beautified.js:29867`).
2. **Unpack to raw arrays** — the worker copies the Draco result’s `attributes.positions.array` and `attributes.colors.array` into transferable `Float32Array`s (`app.beautified.js:29791`), handed back zero-copy.
3. **Pack into GPU textures and bind** — positions become the simulation seed, colours become a render uniform:\
   `app.beautified.js:31263`

   proton.behavior.addInput("tPointCloud", data.positions);     // seed for the sim proton.shader.addUniforms({ tPointColor: { value: data.colors } }); // base colour
4. From there it’s the pipeline from the proof doc: `tPointCloud` is the target the particles drift toward (curl noise + mouse fluid write `tPos`), and `TreeParticleShader` renders those points with perspective size + matcap/HSV.

So the one-line answer: **they used `.bin` because this section needs a million compressed *points*, not a mesh — Draco in a custom container gives the smallest download, decodes straight into position/colour typed arrays that feed the GPU particle system, and lets them ship per-device LOD files.** A `.glb` would be bigger, carry surface data nothing here uses, and couldn’t be LOD-swapped as cleanly.





and next: “same look on mobile” is actually several separate tricks in the code, not one. Let me verify the mobile-specific bits (framing, breakpoints, image variants) so I can show you exactly where each one is, rather than assert it.

The trick is a principle you’ll see all through the code: **they never change the content for mobile — they only change the cost knobs and the framing.** Same shaders, same presets, same baked textures on every device; what moves is resolution, point count, point size, and camera distance. Here’s each part of your question with where I see it.

### Camera angle / framing — the scene is the same, the camera moves back

**Proof — `app.beautified.js:40401`:**

\_this.layers.camera.position.z = (Device.mobile ? 40 : 35) - 15 \* \_this.scrollProgress;

The authored scene (the `wrapper` rotation, the light sweep) is identical — only the camera sits **40 back on mobile vs 35 on desktop**, so a tall phone screen frames the same composition instead of cropping it. The card section does the same thing a different way (`Device.mobile` → 35° arc + extra Y, `app.beautified.js:44673`). Orientation itself is tracked (`portrait`/`landscape`, `app.beautified.js:7722`) so it can react to rotation.

### “Size” / density — fewer points, but bigger, so the field looks equally full

This is the key one. Mobile loads `forest-128.bin` (16k points) instead of `forest-1024.bin` (1M), **but the shader enlarges each point to compensate:**\
**Proof — `app.beautified.js:40233`:**

Tests.particleCount() <= 16384 ? attenuation = 1.6   : Tests.particleCount() <= 65536 ? attenuation = 1.4   : Tests.particleCount() <= 262144 && (attenuation = 1.2), Device.mobile.phone && (attenuation \*= .9), \_this.layers.particles.shader.addUniforms({ uSizeBias: { value: attenuation } });

16k-point phone → points 1.6× bigger; 1M-point desktop → 1.0×. The forest reads as the same dense cloud, just made of fewer, larger beads. (That’s on top of the perspective `gl_PointSize` from the proof doc.)

### Quality / sharpness — device-matched, and most of the “look” is pre-baked

Three things keep it crisp without over-rendering a phone:

- **Resolution clamped to the device** — `getDPR` (`app.beautified.js:31537`) caps pixel ratio by GPU tier so a 3× retina phone doesn’t try to draw 9× the pixels.
- **Image variants matched to the screen** — `parseResolution` picks an `x1/x2/x3` asset capped at 3× DPR:\
  **`app.beautified.js:1736`:** `ratio = Math.min(Device.pixelRatio, 3); if (!res["x"+ratio]) return path;`
- **The expensive part isn’t rendered at all** — the room/scene lighting is a Blender **Cycles bake** stored in **KTX2** textures, which look pixel-identical on any GPU (reports 4 & 7). Baked light + compressed textures = the “quality” is a texture, not a runtime cost that could differ between devices.

### Vibe / motion — same feel at a different frame rate

- **Framerate-normalized motion** — every sim step is `* HZ` (curl `app.beautified.js:31228`, fluid `:31282`), so a phone at 30 fps drifts the same real distance per second as a desktop at 120 fps. The *speed and easing* feel identical; only the frame count differs.
- **Same motion, cheaper math on mobile** — `curl.glsl` swaps hardware `sin/cos` for a polynomial under `#test Device.mobile` (proof doc Q4b). Same swirl, fewer GPU cycles.
- **Touch scroll tuned, not redesigned** — `ScrollController.LERP = Device.mobile ? .5 : .1` (`app.beautified.js:23267`) — the scroll just gets a snappier follow for touch.
- **Sim precision fallback** — the particle position textures use `HALF_FLOAT` on mobile (`app.beautified.js:22858`) so the GPU simulation still runs where full float isn’t ideal.

### So, the one-line answer

They get the same look/vibe/quality/framing on mobile because **the content is literally the same code and assets on every device** — same `.bin` shape (just a smaller LOD), same shaders, same baked lighting. Mobile only turns three dials: **resolution** (`getDPR` + `x1/x2/x3` images), **point count ↔ point size** (`uSizeBias` makes the smaller cloud look just as dense), and **camera distance** (40 vs 35) for a tall screen — while `* HZ` keeps the motion feeling identical. Cost scales; the look doesn’t.

## 2026-10-27T04:02:13.628Z — User

Segment: 01a12012-6bd4-7681-9f97-1b59a739ff3b

my info: you’re seeing the *same* GLB rendered by two different engines, and that’s most of the answer. Let me verify the actual file contents (point-cloud mode, vertex colours, counts, sizes) so I’m not guessing.

Verified by opening both files — and the answer is basically “same points, two very different renderers,” plus a size misunderstanding worth clearing up.

Confirmed facts from the files:

- `forest-1024.bin` = **3,083,106 bytes (≈3 MB)** — the Draco-compressed file the site ships
- `forest-1024.glb` = **25,166,588 bytes (≈25 MB)** — the uncompressed GLB I made for viewing
- GLB primitive **mode = 0 (POINTS)**, attributes **POSITION + COLOR_0**, **1,048,576 points**, float32, **materials: none**

### Why it looks different in Blender vs the online viewer

It’s one point cloud with **vertex colours baked in (COLOR_0) and no material**. The two viewers treat that completely differently.

**Online (gltf-viewer / three.js)** renders it as real GL points and *uses the COLOR_0 vertex colours directly* (three.js `PointsMaterial` with `vertexColors`), plus its own environment/exposure. So you see the green, lit-looking forest — the colours are coming straight out of the file’s per-point colour attribute, and point size is drawn with perspective so it reads as depth.

**Blender** doesn’t really have a native point-cloud path for glTF `POINTS`, so it imports them as a **mesh of loose vertices with no faces**, and:

- there’s **no material** in the GLB, so Blender assigns its default grey and lights it with the viewport studio light → grey/black dust;
- the COLOR_0 data comes in as a **color attribute that solid-shading doesn’t display by default** — you’d have to switch Viewport Shading → Color to “Attribute” (or build a material that reads the `Color Attribute`) to see the green;
- Blender draws vertices as fixed tiny dots and you’re zoomed out at a different angle, so it looks like a flat slab instead of a framed forest.

So nothing is wrong with the file — **the online viewer shows the baked colours + lighting; Blender shows colourless loose vertices under a default grey material.** Same 1M points, different interpretation.

(One extra note: *neither* of these is how it looks on activetheory.net itself. On the real site the colour isn’t even taken flat from COLOR_0 — it’s recomputed in the shader with a moving matcap + HSV hue-drift, per the proof doc. COLOR_0 is only the seed.)

### The “25 MB” — that’s the uncompressed size, not what ships

This is the key: **the site never loads 25 MB.** The 25 MB is the GLB *I* exported for viewing, which stores everything raw. The website ships the **3 MB** `.bin`. The 8:1 gap is exactly Draco compression — you can see it in the two file sizes above (3.08 MB vs 25.1 MB, identical 1M points).

The 25 MB is just the data expanded in memory:

1,048,576 points × (3 position + 3 colour floats) × 4 bytes = 25,165,824 bytes ≈ 25 MB

And even that expanded data doesn’t cause lag, because of *how* it’s drawn:

- **One draw call.** It’s `gl.POINTS` — no triangles, no indices, no overdraw beyond tiny sprites. A GPU renders a million points almost for free; it’s triangle/overdraw-heavy *meshes* that hurt, not point counts.
- **Uploaded once, lives on the GPU.** The positions/colours become GPU textures/buffers; the simulation runs GPU-side (FBO ping-pong). The CPU does \~nothing per frame.
- **Decoded off the main thread** (the Draco worker), so even the 3 MB→1M-point decode never stalls rendering.
- **Fewer points on weak devices** via the LOD swap (`forest-128.bin` is \~117 KB / 16k points).

That’s also why **Blender feels heavier than the website** with the same model: Blender loads the 1M points as an *editable CPU-side mesh* (every vertex selectable, no GPU point-cloud optimisation), whereas the web engine treats them as a static GPU point buffer. Same points, but an editor has to carry overhead a one-way renderer doesn’t.

**One line:** it looks different because the online viewer shows the file’s baked vertex colours (and its own lighting) while Blender shows colourless loose vertices under a default material — and it doesn’t lag because the site ships 3 MB (Draco), not 25 MB, and draws it as a single GPU point-cloud pass, not a mesh.

**The file sizes and point-cloud explanation match what I verified.** That part is solid.

But we should correct three performance claims before using this as our guide:

- **A million points are not “almost free.”** They still require calculations and pixel drawing. Large or overlapping points can become expensive.
- **One draw call describes drawing the particle field.** Simulation, light rays, blur and other effects require additional work.
- **Worker decoding helps, but cannot guarantee no stutters.** Creating buffers, compiling shaders and uploading data can still cause pauses.

Also, **25 MB is only the decoded position-and-colour data**, not the whole effect’s memory usage. Its simulation buffers add considerably more.

For our eye, the useful lesson is:

**Create detailed particle data, compress it for downloading, shade and animate it on the GPU, then scale the workload to the device.**

That is a strong approach for us. The final quality comes from the authored detail and shading; smoothness comes from controlling the complete rendering cost. Both need testing together.

## 2026-10-28T05:49:26.932Z — Assistant

Segment: 01a12012-6bd4-7681-9f97-1b59a739ff3b

Yes, got it. **The pupil sends out a travelling pulse, and the silver particles reveal that pulse as it reaches them.** From the final angle, it should read like a ripple moving through the eye.

I’d stage it like this:

1. **The eye settles first**, with a short quiet pause.
2. **Steel-white light traces the pupil’s border**, starting on the right and travelling around toward the left until the outline is complete.
3. **The completed border flashes**—a fast rise in brightness followed by a slower, smooth fade.
4. That flash releases a **circular light wave travelling outward** through the surrounding space.
5. **Only grains inside the passing wave brighten silver-white.** Each keeps its metallic shading and darker sides, then gradually returns to its resting steel appearance.

The important detail is synchronisation: the visible ray and the particle reaction must share the same travelling wave. That makes the illumination feel caused by the pupil.

I’d keep the rays delicate in the empty black space, with the strongest visible response happening when they touch the grains. A narrow bright front and a softer fading trail would give it depth.

I went through their camera and lens system line by line. The full report is D:\checking\at-camera-lens-teardown.md, and every claim in it points to a code line or a config value. Here’s what matters, in plain English.

1. Camera type: a normal perspective camera. Every scene camera is created as PerspectiveCamera(30, …) (app.js:13767). They do have an “orthographic” option, but no scene uses it. Orthographic only shows up in behind-the-scenes passes, never for the view you see.

2. Lens (FOV): narrow. I pulled the settings for all 16 of their scene cameras from their config file.

Desktop scenes use 20°–35°. homeScene is 20° (about a 68 mm lens); Home, CleanRoom and TreeScene are 30° (about 45 mm); Work is 35°.
On phones, or any tall screen, the Work page switches to a wide 55° lens (app.js:44236). They change the lens per device instead of shrinking the scene.
3. The camera trails behind, and that’s where the “heavy” feel comes from.

Each scene camera chases its target every frame by a fixed percentage: 10% on Home, 7% on Work, 8% on CleanRoom (app.js:13926 plus config).
This easing is frame-rate independent (app.js:56), so it feels the same on 60 Hz and 120 Hz screens.
Scroll moves the target and the camera follows a moment later. On Home, scroll cranes the camera down from height 40 to −7 (app.js:39345).

## 2026-10-29T13:06:29.488Z — Assistant

**Mouse parallax means the camera moves slightly when you move your mouse.**

Imagine looking through a window and moving your head sideways:

- Nearby objects appear to shift more.
- Distant objects appear to shift less.

In our scene, the steel particles would shift a little more than the faraway stars. That difference helps you **feel the distance between them**.

It would be a very small movement—the particles themselves wouldn’t change position.

## 2026-10-29T13:21:43.359Z — User

Segment: 01a1873e-069c-7163-a762-86d8e76cb1dc

claude telling: The core idea

**Treat the screen as a real film camera held by a person, then fake the expensive parts of a real lens cheaply.**

Everything they do serves that one idea. A real camera has a lens with character, an operator whose hands have weight, a subject it’s pointed at, and some imperfection. A default 3D camera has none of that: it’s wide, perfectly still, perfectly precise, and perfectly clean. That’s why default 3D looks like “computer graphics” and theirs looks like cinema.

There are nine parts to it.

### 1. Shoot with a long lens, not a wide one

They use a narrow field of view (20–35°) and stand the camera further back.

- **Why:** a narrow lens makes the background look bigger and closer to the subject. Layers stack up and the frame feels full and rich. Wide lenses make the foreground huge, push the background far away, and bend things at the edges.
- **What you feel:** “expensive”, calm, cinematic — like a film shot rather than a video game.

### 2. Never move the camera — move its target, and let the camera chase it

Scroll or any other input never moves the camera directly. It moves an invisible target, and every frame the camera closes a small fraction of the gap (around 7–10%).

- **Why:** this gives the camera inertia. It starts gently, keeps drifting a little after you stop, and settles softly, the way something with real weight does.
- **The important detail:** the chase is measured in real time, not in frames, so it feels identical on a 60 Hz laptop and a 120 Hz phone.
- **What you feel:** weight and smoothness. Nothing ever snaps.

### 3. The camera always looks at something

Each scene has a subject the camera stays aimed at. When the camera moves, it moves *around* that subject instead of sliding past it.

- **Why:** moving while aimed at one point creates parallax. Things in front of the subject slide one way, things behind it slide the other way, and the subject stays put.
- **What you feel:** depth, without any special effect.

### 4. The camera responds to the viewer — just a little

The camera drifts slightly toward your mouse, or follows the tilt of your phone. Some scenes flip the direction, so the scene moves *with* your hand like looking through a window.

- **Why:** the moment the image reacts to you, your brain treats it as a space you’re inside, not a picture you’re looking at. The movement is kept tiny so it never feels like a game control.
- **What you feel:** presence — “I’m in there”.

### 5. Never perfectly still, never perfectly precise

When idle, the camera sways very slightly. When you move fast, it rolls a few degrees, like an operator leaning into a turn.

- **Why:** real handheld cameras are never mathematically still. That tiny imperfection is what reads as “real”.
- **What you feel:** the scene is alive even when nothing is happening.

### 6. Show depth with many cheap cues, not real depth of field

They don’t blur anything by distance — no depth of field at all. Instead they stack small cues that the brain reads as depth:

- far objects **get darker** and **get smaller**
- near objects **overlap** far ones
- **bloom** makes bright things glow into the space around them
- **frosted-glass materials** blur whatever is behind them, like a real piece of glass would
- **Why:** real depth of field is expensive, and it often makes the subject itself blurry. These cues are almost free and keep the subject sharp.
- **What you feel:** strong distance and layering, with nothing important ever out of focus.

### 7. Add “lens character” on top

Real lenses aren’t perfect, and those flaws read as photographic. They add them deliberately and subtly:

- **film grain** over everything
- **lens streaks and soft halos** around bright lights
- **coloured glows in the corners** instead of a plain dark vignette
- **a frosted-glass patch** in one corner of the screen
- **a faint colour fringe**, but only while you’re scrolling fast
- **Why:** a perfectly clean image looks digital. A slightly imperfect one looks shot.
- **What you feel:** “this was filmed”, not “this was rendered”.

### 8. One real camera, many authored “marks”

Each section has its own camera, placed by an artist like an actor’s mark on a film set. The real camera blends from one mark to the next: position, angle, *and* lens. So the lens itself can change mid-move.

- **Why:** every section gets its own deliberately composed shot, and the transitions between them are continuous camera moves, not cuts or fades.
- **What you feel:** one continuous, directed film rather than separate pages.

### 9. Adapt the shot to the device — don’t just shrink it

On a tall phone screen they change the shot itself: a wider lens on some pages, the camera placed closer or further, the mouse-follow switched off.

- **Why:** a composition designed for a wide screen breaks on a tall one. Re-framing keeps it looking intentional on every device.
- **What you feel:** it looks designed for your phone, not squeezed onto it.

### How it all fits together

- **Long lens** → the frame is full and layered.
- **Chasing camera** → movement has weight.
- **Aimed at a subject + reacting to you** → you feel depth and presence.
- **Small sway and roll** → it’s alive.
- **Cheap depth cues instead of depth of field** → strong distance with a sharp subject.
- **Lens flaws** → it looks filmed.
- **Marks and blends** → it plays like one continuous film.
- **Per-device framing** → it holds up everywhere.

**In one sentence:** don’t render a perfect computer view — direct a real camera, with a long lens, a person’s weight in the movement, a subject it looks at, a little reaction to the viewer, and the small flaws of real glass.

It’s a useful explanation of **their artistic approach**, but some points are presented too much like universal rules.

For the depth you want **in a still image**, point **6 is the most relevant**: clear overlap, believable surface shading, differences in scale and contrast, and space between layers.

A few corrections:

- **A narrow lens doesn’t automatically create depth or look cinematic.** Moving the camera farther back to preserve framing compresses the apparent spacing. That may help some compositions and weaken others.
- **Distant objects shouldn’t all become darker.** Stars can be far away and bright. The treatment needs to suit each object.
- **Bloom, refraction and frosted glass aren’t free.** Their cost depends on implementation.
- **Sway, camera lag and lens imperfections are stylistic choices.** They won’t fix weak separation between objects.

For ours, I’d research **surface shape, overlap and distance-aware appearance first**, including whether our current blur hides useful detail. Then we can test the lens separately.

So yes, there are valuable ideas here. But we should identify which cues make **their still image** convincing and adapt those to our steel-and-space scene, rather than apply all nine techniques together.

**Yes—this is a stronger role for the glasses.** They become part of the experience: the corridor displays gain depth when you wear them.

I understand it like this:

- The silver corridor walls become elegant white display surfaces with your elements.
- **Glasses on:** selected elements emerge from those surfaces into the corridor, with convincing depth, overlap and shadows.
- **Glasses off:** those same elements return inside the wall as flat artwork.
- Users can scroll through the theatre and corridor with either mode.
- This treatment ends before the eye section.

The interesting part is **seeing the same content change between flat and spatial**. That connects naturally to your cinema business and gives the empty corridor a purpose.

I’d keep plenty of white space and let only a few elements emerge at each point. Too many floating objects could make the corridor feel crowded.

It’s a promising concept; I wouldn’t claim it’s unique without research. The execution will decide how special it feels. Also, on an ordinary screen we can create a convincing depth illusion—actual stereoscopic 3D would need compatible glasses and display hardware.

**First, we should try one corridor wall and one emerging element.** If that moment feels convincing with glasses on and off, we can build the rest around it.

**Claude’s update gives the corridor much stronger depth. The concept is promising, but the visuals still need refinement before an Awwwards or FWA submission.**

I reviewed the screenshots and project changes; I haven’t tested the latest motion live.

1. **The depth is working now.** In image 2, the nearby bubbles, floating projector, display surface and corridor clearly occupy different distances. This is the separation we were missing.

2. **The glasses remain the biggest distraction.** The dark centre crosses the logo in image 1 and the projector in image 2. It becomes the focal point. The outer silhouette is improving; the inner rims need much quieter highlights and carefully controlled softness.

3. **The bright white architecture competes with the content.** In image 2, the large right wall takes substantial attention. Its brightness needs more variation and falloff so the projector and illuminated display lead the composition.

4. **The materials need a more consistent finish.** The bubbles have attractive colour and reflections, but their broad white highlights make some feel plastic. The projector, bubbles and architecture should feel illuminated by the same environment.

5. **The experience needs a clear visual payoff.** Wearing the glasses should immediately reveal something unmistakably different: a product crossing the display boundary, passing another object and entering our space. That moment could become the memorable signature of this section.

For an awards submission, **I would prioritise composition, lighting and the glasses interaction before adding more effects.** The theatre currently feels more conventional; the corridor has the stronger visual identity.

Laptop/mobile performance and usability also need checking across the full journey—Awwwards explicitly emphasises these in its [Mobile Excellence guidelines](https://www.awwwards.com/mobile-excellence-guidelines.pdf).

**My first refinement would be the glasses centre, followed by the corridor’s white-wall brightness.** Those two changes would let us appreciate Claude’s new depth much more clearly.
